rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic sequence evokes the whole history of guidance: Muhammad's opponents receive the guidance given to earlier peoples, and persistent rejection will bring them the fate of earlier deniers.
rows.anchor: the whole sequence of guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Furqān is the standard distinguishing good from evil; here it is the Torah, formerly God's Book, and the Qur'an receives the same name because God's Book sets that standard.
rows.anchor: the standard that distinguishes good from evil. Here it refers to the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍiyāʾ and nūr mean light; God's Book rescues people from mental, moral, ideological, and practical quagmires and brings them into light.
rows.anchor: are used for the Book of God because it delivers people from mental, moral, ideological and practical quagmires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr means reminder; here the Torah reminds people of truths grounded in themselves, their surroundings, and history, as the Qur'an is called elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Since these scriptures remind people of various facts based on the world within them and that around them as well as on history

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like the Torah, the Qur'an benefits people whose innate intellectual and natural light remains alive; these people fear God and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: They are ones who fear God and the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an, like the Torah, is revealed as a blessing for everyone, but only those with the capacity to receive it benefit.
rows.anchor: Though, like the rain of mercy, it is a blessing for everyone, only they will benefit from it who have the ability.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's closing address to Quraysh asks them to reflect on what they are actually denying.
rows.anchor: they are told they should contemplate what they are really denying.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is mentioned briefly because his account was treated in detail in the previous section; the narrative now turns to Abraham in detail.
rows.anchor: For this reason, here it is briefly referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rushd means guidance and comprehension of God.
rows.anchor: means “guidance and comprehension of God.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative pronoun in the phrase makes the grant specific: God gave Abraham the guidance and comprehension he was worthy of.
rows.anchor: The way it occurs with an accusative pronoun here has incorporated a special meaning in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance has degrees, and God bestows it in proportion to each person's abilities and status; Abraham's particular share is identified with 2:124.
rows.anchor: There are various stages of this guidance and comprehension. The Almighty bestows it in proportion to a person’s abilities in accordance with his status.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's high rank followed stringent trials; Islahi rebukes those who claim his lineage and status without practicing even his easiest ways, since God grants status according to merit and capacity.
rows.anchor: after he proved worthy of it by passing through very stringent trials.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recalled incident occurred earlier in Abraham's life and displays his courage together with the guidance and understanding God granted him.
rows.anchor: It shows his bravery and courage as well as the guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham came from an idol-worshipping family whose father carved idols, yet God blessed him with monotheism that continues to illuminate the world until Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: he was blessed with the light of monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's question humiliates the idols, and the term for being devoted to them carries sarcasm about his father's and people's obtuseness.
rows.anchor: The humiliation they carry for the idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only someone specially blessed by God, whose faith is majestic and free of fear or greed, could proclaim monotheism at such a young age.
rows.anchor: At such a tender age, only that person can raise this slogan of monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Appeal to forefathers is a powerful defense of foolish practice for common people because it stirs tribal solidarity and communal honor, making a different path hard to adopt.
rows.anchor: It appeals to their sentiments of tribal support and communal honour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tradition does not turn an inherited mistake into guidance; people must assess it through human nature and intellect.
rows.anchor: it must be judged on the basis of human nature and intellect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ḥaqq means something serious and considered.
rows.anchor: means something that is serious and well thought of.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's people found his declaration so strange that they assumed he was a young man speaking impulsively, and treated it as jest to blunt its effect on the masses.
rows.anchor: They thought that he was a young man with a raw mind and had said something impulsively without giving it any serious thought.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham answers that stone-carved idols cannot be lords: their Lord is the Creator of the heavens and earth, whom he publicly proclaims.
rows.anchor: their stone-carved idols cannot be their Lord; in fact, their Lord is the God of the heavens and the earth Who has created them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shahādah here means a declaration and proclamation, a sense used elsewhere in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: here refers to a declaration and proclamation. It is used in this meaning at several instances in the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayd is a concealed measure or step taken against a rival.
rows.anchor: It refers to a measure or a step done against a rival in secret.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about the people leaving shows that Abraham spoke in a gathering inside the temple, hinted at his intention, and concealed the actual scheme to be revealed later.
rows.anchor: when you leave from here and go away” that Abraham (sws) had made this assertion in some gathering within the temple.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode continues Abraham's method described in 6:76–79: subtle sarcasm and gradual reasoning guide listeners to a conclusion that leaves them speechless and conceding defeat.
rows.anchor: he would also try to lead his addressees gradually to the conclusion he wanted them to grasp.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At night Abraham smashed the idols except the largest, intending to blame it and ask whether it could speak; their admission that idols cannot explain or prevent harm would expose them as false gods.
rows.anchor: Grabbing an opportunity at night time, he smashed the idols into small pieces and just left the large one intact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judhādh refers to something smashed into bits and pieces.
rows.anchor: refers to something that has been smashed to bits and pieces.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broken idols complete Abraham's hidden plan: if they cannot speak, he can decisively ask how they can be gods.
rows.anchor: when these small and big idols cannot speak, how can they regard them to be their deities?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse consists of two sentences: the first conveys amazement and anxiety, while the second conveys anger and fury.
rows.anchor: This verse is composed of two separate sentences. Their amazement and anxiety is evident from the first, and their anger and fury from the second.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People familiar with Abraham's views, message, and challenge infer that he damaged the idols because they had heard him speak of them contemptuously.
rows.anchor: because they had heard him mention these idols in a degrading way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people leave the derogatory description implicit, suppressing the word “degrading” in their answer.
rows.anchor: They suppressed the word “degrading”
